system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2192-03-23 13:27:00 to 2192-03-25 20:04:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, prior stents, diabetes, and diastolic heart failure was admitted for chest pain concerning for unstable angina. Initial evaluation showed no myocardial infarction, with normal troponins and ECG. He underwent cardiac catheterization, which revealed significant diffuse disease in the LAD artery. He successfully underwent percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA) of the LAD without stent placement. He remained chest pain-free post-procedure, with stable vital signs and improved renal function. His home medications, including dual antiplatelet therapy, statin, beta-blocker, and antihypertensives, were continued. He was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up instructions for cardiology and primary care, and guidance on medication adherence and symptom monitoring.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ man with history of pleuritic chest pain, assess for
pneumonia.  

COMPARISON:  Prior exam is dated ___ and a prior CT torso from ___.  

FINDINGS:

PA and lateral views of the chest were provided demonstrating no focal
consolidation effusion or pneumothorax.  A stent projecting over the heart on
the lateral projection corresponds with a stent residing within the circumflex
coronary artery.  The cardiomediastinal silhouette is stable.  Bony structures
are intact.  

IMPRESSION:

No acute intrathoracic process.

HISTORY:  History of intermittent chest pain radiating to the back.  Evaluate
for dissection.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT axial imaging was obtained through the chest following the
administration of intravenous contrast material according to the chest pain
protocol.  Coronal and sagittal reformats were completed. Oblique reformats
were completed.

DLP: 518.

COMPARISON:  CT torso from ___.

FINDINGS:

CT chest with contrast:  The thyroid gland is unremarkable.  There are no
enlarged supraclavicular, axillary, mediastinal or hilar lymph nodes.  There
is a normal 3 vessel aortic arch.  The aorta is of normal caliber without
evidence of acute aortic pathology including dissection.  The main pulmonary
artery is of normal caliber and there is no pulmonary embolus.  Coronary
stents are noted.  There is no pericardial effusion.  The heart is not
enlarged.  Scattered small ground-glass opacities in the right lower lobe
(3:117) in a subpleural peribronchovascular distribution with a single
mucus-plugged small airway and other areas of bronchiectasis in the right
lower lobe suggests acute on chronic airways infection. There is minimal
atelectasis in the right middle lobe and right base.  There is no large focal
consolidation, pleural effusion or pneumothorax.  The airways are patent the
subsegmental levels.

This study is not tailored for evaluation of subdiaphragmatic structures but
limited views are unremarkable.

Osseous structures:  There are no concerning osseous lesions.

IMPRESSION:
1. No evidence of pulmonary embolism or acute aortic pathology.

2. Scattered small ground-glass opacities in the right lower lobe with a mucus
plgged airway and bronchiectasis suggests acute on chronic airways infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Patel. You came in with chest pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started three days ago while I was sleeping. It's a pressure on the left side, and it gets worse when I breathe in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Does the pain go anywhere else? Any sweating, nausea, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No sweating or fever. I’ve felt a little nauseous but no vomiting. It’s not worse with activity, and it feels different from my past heart attacks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. We’ve checked your EKG and blood work. Your troponin is normal, which is good—no sign of a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what could it be? It hurts every time I take a deep breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because it’s worse with breathing and not typical for a heart attack, we’re considering pericarditis— inflammation around the heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Inflammation? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but often it’s mild and gets better with treatment. We’re giving you nitroglycerin and starting heparin and metoprolol just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another procedure like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your cardiac cath from last month showed stable disease. We don’t think this is related to blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about the CT scan they mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT to rule out blood clots or aortic issues. No pulmonary embolism or dissection. Your lungs look mostly clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a chest X-ray. No pneumonia or fluid. So pericarditis is still the top possibility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How will you confirm that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do an echocardiogram to check for fluid around the heart and a nuclear stress test to rule out ischemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your echo came back. No new wall motion issues and no pericardial effusion. Your heart function is still 55%, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no fluid? Does that rule out pericarditis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not entirely. You can have pericarditis without fluid. The pain with breathing and the EKG change support it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the plan then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring your troponins. If they stay negative and the stress test is normal, we’ll treat it as pericarditis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your second troponin was negative, and the nuclear stress test was normal—no signs of reduced blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart arteries?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Your stents are open, and there’s no new blockage. We’re confident this is pericarditis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What causes that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often viral, but sometimes it follows heart procedures or occurs without a clear cause. Given your history, we think it’s likely viral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, usually within a week or two. We’re giving you acetaminophen for pain. We avoid NSAIDs because of your heart history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take the oxycodone if it’s really bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can use oxycodone as needed for pain, but we prefer acetaminophen as the main treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my other medicines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on your usual meds: metoprolol, diltiazem, valsartan, insulin, and atorvastatin. We added metformin for diabetes control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my heart failure okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re not retaining fluid. You’re euvolemic, so we’ll keep your Lasix as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is much better today. You’re breathing easier and the exam shows no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it still hurts a little when I breathe deep, but much less than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We’re discharging you today. Continue acetaminophen every six hours for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can use it as needed, but try to limit it. Also, keep taking all your heart and diabetes meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Weigh yourself daily. Call if you gain more than three pounds in a day. Also, if chest pain changes or worsens, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, see your cardiologist in one week. We’ll send them a summary. Keep your primary care visit too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, prior stents, diabetes, and diastolic heart failure was admitted for pleuritic chest pain lasting three days. The pain was positional and worse with inspiration, differing from prior myocardial infarctions. Initial evaluation showed normal troponins, no EKG evidence of acute ischemia, and a normal echocardiogram. A nuclear stress test was normal, and imaging ruled out pulmonary embolism and aortic dissection. The clinical picture was consistent with pericarditis. The patient responded well to acetaminophen and symptom management, with no complications. Chronic conditions including diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and heart failure were managed with continued medications. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions for pain control, weight monitoring, and cardiology follow-up.
